analysis.one_liner: Applies Social Security payroll tax to high wages above the annual cap, plus strengthens the fund's paper backing.
analysis.headline: No cosponsors ever joined and the Ways and Means Committee never acted on the bill, which died at the end of the 111th Congress without a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Social Security taxes apply only to wages up to an annual cap (about $106,800 in 2009); income above that goes untaxed for the program. This bill would add a new 3% tax on both workers and employers for every dollar above that cap, with a 6% version for self-employed people. The extra money would flow into Social Security. The bill also required Treasury securities to carry facsimile signatures of the President and Treasury Secretary — a symbolic measure meant to emphasize the realness of the bonds in the Social Security trust fund. Its text says the new taxes would begin after December 31, 2009.
analysis.who_benefits: Social Security beneficiaries and future retirees gain a stronger-financed program, since the new tax on high earners' wages would raise additional dedicated revenue for the trust funds. Most workers' own paycheck taxes would not change, because only wages above the annual cap would be taxed at the new rate.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Current and future Social Security beneficiaries

how_it_helps.text: Adds a new 3% payroll tax (6% for self-employment income) on every dollar of wages above the Social Security contribution and benefit base, the annual cap on wages subject to Social Security tax.
The revenue would support Social Security's finances, since employment taxes under the Federal Insurance Contributions Act fund the program.

Requires Treasury obligations to bear facsimile signatures of the President and Treasury Secretary, a symbolic gesture tied to public debate over whether the bonds in the Social Security trust fund are real assets.

analysis.who_pays: High-earning workers, employers of high earners, and high-earning self-employed people would pay the new tax, roughly 3% of the employer side and 3% of the employee side on wages above the cap. Some of the employer share could indirectly reduce wages or hiring at the top over time, but the direct cost falls on payroll above roughly $106,000 per worker.
analysis.who_pays_short: Workers and employers above the wage cap

drawbacks.text: The new tax applies only to wages, not investment income, so it does not touch the income sources of the very wealthiest households, whose income is largely capital gains and dividends.
A 6% combined additional tax on high earners' wages is a substantial new payroll burden, and the employer share could offset raises or hiring for workers above the cap.
The signature requirement on Treasury securities is largely symbolic and does not itself affect the trust fund's finances.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would modestly strengthen Social Security's financing by asking people with above-cap wages — roughly the top earners — to pay more into the program. Its weakness is that it taxes only wages, so it leaves untouched the capital income where most top-decile wealth accumulates, and the symbolic signature provision does little. The cost would fall on a narrow group, and no one testified or scored the bill in committee, so its practical economic effects were never evaluated.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, never got a hearing or a markup, and expired at the end of the 111th Congress.

narrative.text: Rep. Robert Wexler introduced the bill on April 1, 2009, and it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day.
No cosponsors signed on to the bill during its entire life.
The Ways and Means Committee never reported the bill, and it received no floor vote before the Congress ended in January 2011.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High earners and their employers were better off because the bill died: the 3% tax on wages above the Social Security cap never took effect. Social Security's trust funds did not receive the additional revenue the bill would have provided.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High earners above the payroll tax cap

for.name: Rep. Robert Wexler
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to Ways and Means; it drew no cosponsors in the two years before he left office.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral, holding no hearing or markup, leaving it to die when the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No cosponsors joined from either party and the committee never acted, so there is no record of partisan division — only of silence.

industries.industry: High-earning wage earners and their employers
industries.note: Would have paid a new 3% tax (6% combined for self-employed) on wages above the Social Security cap, roughly $106,800 in 2009. The cost falls on a narrow slice of the workforce, not on ordinary payroll.
Would have received the new dedicated payroll tax revenue, improving long-term program finances.
